newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Business as usual in Pakistan after Bhutto sacked.
newsitem.headline: Business as usual in Pakistan after Bhutto sacked.

text.p: Small groups of soldiers guarded key buildings in Pakistan's capital on Tuesday, but the city was calm and some residents rejoiced after the president dismissed Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto with an overnight proclamation.
Children walked to school and residents went about their business on a crisp, sunny morning. Many expressed satisfaction at President Farooq Leghari's decision to sack Bhutto.
"We are feeling very happy," said Khalid Mehmood, 28, as he flipped "puris", or fried bread, at his shop in Aabpara market. Elated shopkeepers set off fire crackers at Melody market.
A handful of army trucks entered the city in the early hours, soon after Leghari issued an order dissolving the lower house of parliament and calling elections for next February.
Deputy police chief Raja Saleem told Reuters that a small number of police officers equipped with riot gear had been deployed in the capital on Monday evening.

There were no reports of violence and only small numbers of soldiers were deployed at sensitive spots, including the state-run radio and television stations, the telecommunications company, cabinet offices and the prime minister's secretariat.
Bhutto was in her official residence, located on a low hill overlooking a sprawling complex of marble government buildings.
A police officer guarding the entrance to her residence said: "Everything is OK. Khalid is going to take over."
He was referring to former National Assembly speaker Meraj Khalid, who Leghari named as caretaker prime minister.
A lone military jeep was parked outside the prime minister's secretariat.
Cars and buses plied Islamabad's streets and workers were entering government buildings. The city's airport was open.

In the southern city of Karachi, Pakistan's financial and commercial hub, there was no unusual movement of security forces, and business and trade carried on. The Karachi bourse was closed for a previously scheduled one-day holiday.
Business executive Shahid Amin, speaking from Lahore, welcomed Bhutto's dismissal. "It means that the business atmosphere will improve," he told Reuters by telephone.
At Aabpara, Islamabad's oldest market and the focal point of a demonstration last week against Bhutto's government, residents were elated.
"We are so happy because the government was corrupt," Ishtiaq Khattak, a 23-year-old student, said. "Today is a very happy day for the Pakistan nation."
Several residents cited inflation as their main concern.
"There have been lots of price hikes and unemployment, and industries have been shut," said Mohammad Azin, a 65-year-old retired government accountant.
"Price hikes have been loaded on to the backs of the poor people," said Ahmed Khan, a 33-year-old garment salesman.
Residents hailed Leghari, who at one time was a close Bhutto ally in her Pakistan People's Party.
"No one was expecting this from him as he was a party worker," said the white-bearded Azin. "This step proves that what he did is for the larger benefit of the nation."
